title: Event-driven architecture and event sourcing
subtitle: Events can tell other services what changed, carry the data with them, or become your database. Know which one you are building, and what each costs.

c.v: In 2019, engineer Chris Kiehl wrote up a year of running an
event-sourced
system in production. He had made the design call, and his team built it from scratch in Java.
The pitch had been simple. Every change is an event in a log. Any service can subscribe and react. You get an audit log and time travel for free.

The real system was different. In his view, letting services read each other's raw events was both "extremely coupled" and "excruciatingly opaque". It became hard to tell which services produced or consumed which events.

About a month in, a change in focus made some stored events "no longer relevant, at all". The team had to either translate old events on read or rewrite the log. Either way, he writes, they could no longer reproduce exactly how the system looked before the change.
He also warns about the next stage. Once the data grows, reads must move to projections. Those lag behind writes, so new items can return 404 and deleted items can stay visible for a while.
His advice at the end: ask what core problem event sourcing solves for you. If you cannot answer clearly, a history table or a plain queue may be enough.
"Event-driven" means at least three different things. Martin Fowler separates them.
Kiehl's own closing question points at this mix-up: "Is what you actually want just a plain old queue?"
Event notification
A service sends an event to say "something changed". It does not expect a reply. The receiver calls back if it needs details.
Event-carried state transfer
The event carries the changed data. Receivers keep their own copy, so they never need to call the sender.
Event sourcing.
Every change to your own data is stored as an event. The
event store
is the main source of truth. Current state is whatever you get by replaying the events.
The first two are about how services talk. The third is about how one service stores its data. You can use the first two without the third.
The key idea.

Events between services are messages. Event sourcing makes events your database. The first is common and useful. The second is a big, hard-to-undo decision for the parts of a system that need full history.
Events between services
Event notification gives low
coupling
. The sender does not know who listens.
Microsoft adds that you can add new consumers without changing the producer.
The cost is that the flow is hidden. Fowler warns that "it can be hard to see such a flow as it's not explicit in any program text".
Debugging is harder too, because there is no shared call stack. Put a
correlation ID
in every event so you can link the steps into one
trace
Event-carried state transfer gives more resilience. Receivers keep working when the sender is down, and they need no remote call. The cost is many copies of the data.
Those copies are
eventually consistent
. For a while after an event, different services see different states.
The
sagas, outbox and CDC lesson
shows how to publish these events safely.
Event sourcing: the stream is the truth
In event sourcing, each aggregate (an account, an order) has its own stream. A stream is the ordered list of every event for that one object.
You never update or delete an event. To undo a change, you append a new event that reverses it.
This is the same rule as a
double-entry ledger
, applied to any kind of data.
To load an aggregate, you start from an empty state and apply every event in order.
Fowler calls the full version a "complete rebuild". You can also stop at a past time to see the state as it was then.
Step through one account stream. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Appending with an expected version
Two requests can load the same stream at the same moment and both pass your rules. Event stores stop this with
optimistic concurrency control
. They reject an append if the stream changed since it was read. The loser reloads, checks again, and
retries
Purpose-built stores support this directly. In KurrentDB you pass the revision you read as the expected stream state. If the stream is not in that state, the append throws an error.
In Postgres you can get the same result with a
primary key
on
(stream_id, version)
If another writer already saved the next version, the insert breaks the primary key. Postgres reports that as error code 23505,
unique_violation
The caller catches
ConflictError
, loads again, and retries. Always pass the version you loaded. This check only proves that the next version is free.
Snapshots
Long streams are slow to replay. A snapshot is a saved copy of the state at one version, taken every N events. To load, you read the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it.
Snapshots are only a speed-up. The stream stays the truth, and you can rebuild any snapshot from it.
Replay and the outside world

Replaying must not repeat side effects. If a replay calls the payment provider or sends emails again, real people are affected. Fowler suggests a gateway in front of each outside system that knows when it is in replay mode and skips the call.
Versioning old events
Events live forever, but your code changes. Microsoft lists four strategies, which you can use alone or together.
Tolerant deserialization.
Ignore unknown fields and default missing ones. This handles fields you add.
Event versioning.
A version number in each event, so the reader picks the right logic.
Upcasting
Functions convert old event shapes to the current one when they are read. Stored events stay unchanged.
In-place migration.
Rewrite stored events to the new shape. Use this only as a last resort, because it breaks the audit trail.
The general rules for changing data formats are in
schema evolution and encoding
. Kiehl's story shows the limit. Upcasting keeps your code working, but a change in what an event
means
can still blur the past.
Deleting personal data
Laws like the "right to be forgotten" clash with a store that never deletes. Microsoft's first advice is to keep personal data outside the event store and refer to it by ID.
If you cannot, use
crypto-shredding
. You encrypt each person's data with their own key. To forget them, you delete the key.
It adds encryption work on every read and write, and needs careful key management.
Verraes notes that it only helps if consumers such as projections also keep the data encrypted. It does not cover values that consumers computed from the data.

Verraes also asks whether this counts as deletion under GDPR. An update to his post quotes a reader whose lawyer said it does not. That reader prefers keeping personal data in a separate store you can delete from.
Read models
Replaying a stream on every query is slow, so you build
read models
(projections) that are updated from the events. They lag behind writes.
The next lesson,
CQRS
and read models
, covers them.
CRUD + history table
Partial. You log what you choose.
Low.
Most services, including admin screens and settings.
Event notification
Hidden flows, and callbacks to the sender.
Other services need to react, but can fetch details.
Event-carried state transfer
Many copies of data, eventually consistent.
Receivers must keep working when the sender is down.
Event sourcing
Every change, in order.
Versioning, snapshots, replay safety, projections, and new skills for the team.
Ledgers, orders and other areas where history and audit are core business needs.

Microsoft's summary: for most systems, and most parts of a system, plain data storage is enough. Its poor fits include simple CRUD, short-lived prototypes, systems that need real-time consistent views, mostly static data, and teams new to event-driven design.
Apply event sourcing to the few parts that need it, not to the whole system.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: When someone says "event-driven", ask:
"Notification, state transfer, or event sourcing?"
Then argue about one thing at a time.
Before you event-source anything, write down the core problem it solves. If the answer is "audit", ask whether a history table is enough.
Name events for business intent, like
SeatsReserved
, not "remaining seats changed to 42".
Do not let other services read your raw stored events. Publish separate integration events as your public contract. Microsoft notes that stored events are often too low-level for this.
Always append with an expected version. Test what happens when two writers race.
Plan event versioning and personal data on day one. Both are painful to add later.
Put a correlation ID in every event, and check that your tracing follows it.
"Here is our event-sourced Account aggregate. Write a test where two writers load version 3 and both append. Assert that exactly one succeeds and the other gets a conflict error."
"List every event type in this codebase. For each one, say whether it is a notification, carries state, or is a stored domain event. Mark any stored event that another service reads directly."
"We renamed
amount
to
amount_paise
in the Deposited event. Write an upcaster for old events, and a test that replays a stream with both versions."
The append really checks the expected version. An agent may write a plain insert with no unique key, which quietly allows
lost updates
Replays and projection rebuilds do not call outside systems or send messages.
No migration edits stored events in place. Old shapes are handled by upcasters.
Personal data is either outside the store or encrypted with a per-person key.
Event handlers are
idempotent
, since delivery is usually
at-least-once

q.v: The Orders service publishes "OrderPlaced" with only the order ID. Shipping then calls the Orders API to get the address. Which pattern is this?

why.v: The event only says that something changed. The receiver must call back for the data it needs.

q.v: Two requests load the same account stream at version 7. Both append a withdrawal with expected version 7. What should the event store do?

options.v: Save the first as version 8 and reject the second, which must reload and decide again.
Save the second and drop the first.

why.v: The expected-version check is optimistic concurrency. The second writer's view is out of date, so its append fails.

q.v: You renamed a field in the "Deposited" event. Old events in the store still use the old name. What is the usual fix?

options.v: Edit every old event in the store to the new shape.
Add an upcaster that converts old events to the new shape when they are read.
Delete the old events and keep a snapshot.

why.v: Upcasting keeps stored events unchanged. Rewriting history breaks the audit trail and should be a last resort.

q.v: A team wants to event-source its admin settings screen "for the audit log". Nothing else needs history or replay. What should a senior suggest?

options.v: Event-source it, since every system benefits from an audit log.
Keep it as CRUD and add a history table.

why.v: Simple CRUD with no need for replay or history is a clear case where event sourcing does not pay off. A history table gives the audit trail cheaply.
